newsitem.title: UK: Queen Elizabeth's husband savaged for gun comments.
newsitem.headline: Queen Elizabeth's husband savaged for gun comments.

text.p: Britain's Prince Philip was savaged by his critics on Thursday after he attacked government plans to ban most handguns, saying members of shooting clubs were no more dangerous than golfers or cricketers.

Philip, 75, the blunt-spoken husband of Queen Elizabeth, expressed sympathy for the relatives of 16 children killed by a lone gunman in the Scottish town of Dunblane in March but said public and government reaction had not been wholly rational. "If a cricketer, for instance, suddenly decided to go into a school and batter a lot of people to death with a cricket bat, which he could do very easily, I mean are you going to ban cricket bats?" he said in a BBC radio interview.
His comments, due to be broadcast on Thursday night, come in the wake of an outpouring of public anger and grief after loner Thomas Hamilton shot the children and their teacher in March.
Many condemned the Duke for trying to draw similarities between handguns and cricket bats and making the comments just before the first Christmas in Dunblane since the killings.

"How many people can you kill in three and a half minutes with a cricket bat? It is not the same as an automatic gun. You have to be realistic," said Beverley Birnie, whose six-year-old son Matthew survived the shootings at Dunblane.
Tony Blair, leader of the opposition Labour party, told BBC television the Duke's analogy had been unwise but other members of his party were less restrained.
"I despair of the Duke of Edinburgh. This man is insensitive, selfish and ham-fisted," said Labour member of parliament Tony Banks.
"Once again he has wandered into a highly sensitive area. A prolonged period of silence on his part would be much appreciated," said Banks.

Members of the royal family are not supposed to dabble in politics and government ministers are unlikely to be impressed by his criticism of their planned legislation, which itself was attacked for being too timid.
"Quite honestly, I don't see this sort of legislation preventing handguns getting into the hands of criminals. I mean, it didn't before and it's not going to do now," said Philip.
A Buckingham Palace spokesman said the Duke had not wanted to distress anyone but the statement did little to fend off the growing outrage.

"To think of the Queen coming up here and laying a wreath at our school and then hearing her husband say something like this sickens me," said Ann Pearston, an organiser of Dunblane's Snowdrop Campaign which aims to ban all handguns.
Shooting groups welcomed the Duke's comments but their voices were largely drowned out.

The Duke has a history of making controversial comments. During a visit to China in 1986 he described Peking as "ghastly" and told British students: "If you stay here much longer you'll all be slitty-eyed."
In 1995 he asked a Scottish driving instructor: "How do you keep the natives off the booze (drink) long enough to pass the test?"
